name: Prime Gaming (Easy Version)
description: This is the easy version of the problem. The difference between the versions is that in this version, $$$m \le 2$$$. You can hack only if you solved all versions of this problem. A valid configuration is defined as an arrangement of $$$n$$$ piles of stones such that: The number of stones in each pile is an integer between $$$1$$$ and $$$m$$$ (both inclusive). Given a valid configuration of $$$n$$$ piles of stones, some indices from $$$1$$$ to $$$n$$$ are marked as good . Alice and Bob start playing a game taking $$$n-1$$$ turns alternately with Alice going first. In each turn, they have to perform the following operation: Choose any integer $$$i$$$ such that $$$1 \le i \le p$$$ (where $$$p$$$ is the number of piles left) and $$$i$$$ is good , and remove the $$$i$$$-th pile completely. Note that after performing the operation once, the number of piles decreases by $$$1$$$ and the remaining piles are re-indexed. The game will end when there is only one pile left. It is guaranteed that the index $$$1$$$ is always good. Let $$$x$$$ denote the number of stones in the final remaining pile. Alice wants to maximize $$$x$$$, whereas Bob wants to minimize it. Both Alice and Bob play optimally. Find the sum of $$$x$$$ over all the possible valid configurations modulo $$$10 ^ 9 + 7$$$.
input_specification: Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases $$$t$$$ ($$$1 \le t \le 10^4$$$). The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each testcase contains two integers $$$n$$$ ($$$1 \le n \le 20$$$) and $$$m$$$ ($$$1 \le m \le 2$$$) — the number of piles and the upper bound on the number of stones in a pile. The second line of each testcase contains a single integer $$$k$$$ ($$$1 \le k \le n$$$) — the number of indices marked as good. The third line of each testcase contains $$$k$$$ integers $$$c_1,c_2,\ldots,c_k$$$ ($$$1=c_1 \lt c_2 \lt \ldots \lt c_k\le n$$$) — the good indices. It is guaranteed that $$$1$$$ is always a good index (i.e. $$$c_1=1$$$) . It is guaranteed that the sum of $$$2^n$$$ over all test cases does not exceed $$$2^{20}$$$. It is guaranteed that the sum of $$$m$$$ over all test cases does not exceed $$$10^6$$$.
output_specification: For each testcase, print a single integer — the sum of $$$x$$$ over all the possible valid configurations modulo $$$10 ^ 9 + 7$$$.
approach_summary: Define state dp[mask][i] capturing the subset of visited/chosen elements. Transition by iterating over valid unset bits in O(2^N × N) time.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 2140E1 — Prime Gaming (Easy Version) [450. Bitmask DP]
topic_editorial.summary: Bitmask DP state compression over subsets.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: Because the dimension $N$ is small ($N \le 20$), each subset of chosen or visited elements can be encoded compactly into a single bitmask integer $0 \le \text{mask} < 2^N$. The optimal substructure property guarantees that to extend a subset $\text{mask}$, we only need to know the current subset and optionally the last added element.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: State Definition
Define $dp[\text{mask}]$ (or $dp[\text{mask}][u]$ if the last visited element matters) as:
- $dp[\text{mask}] = $ the optimal value obtainable using the subset of elements represented by the bitmask $\text{mask}$.

### Step 2: Base Cases
- Initialize all DP states to a sentinel value (e.g. $\infty$ for minimization, or $-\infty$ for maximization).
- Base state: $dp[0] = 0$ (empty configuration has cost zero).

### Step 3: Recurrence Relation & Transitions
For every mask from $0$ to $2^N - 1$:
If the state $dp[\text{mask}]$ is reachable:
For every element $i \in [0, N-1]$ such that the $i$-th bit is NOT set in $\text{mask}$ ($(\text{mask} \mathbin{\&} (1 \ll i)) == 0$):
$$\text{next\_mask} = \text{mask} \mid (1 \ll i)$$
$$dp[\text{next\_mask}] = \text{opt}\big(dp[\text{next\_mask}], dp[\text{mask}] + \text{cost}(\text{mask}, i)\big)$$

### Step 4: Final Answer
The final answer is stored in $dp[(1 \ll N) - 1]$, which corresponds to all $N$ elements being chosen.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(2^N \cdot N)$
  There are $2^N$ total bitmasks. From each mask, we iterate over at most $N$ possible next bits to transition. For $N = 20$, $2^{20} \cdot 20 \approx 2 \times 10^7$ operations, which easily runs in $\approx 0.15$ seconds.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(2^N)$
  Storing the DP table for all $2^N$ configurations requires $2^{20} \times 8$ bytes $\approx 8\text{ MB}$ of memory, well below 256 MB.
